title: Mostly quiet
hookLine: speak rarely and only what's needed, and not about people (Enchiridion 33)

lines: HOW MUCH TALK WAS ABOUT SOMEONE ELSE?
cards: Three hundred sixty-five. A whole calendar's worth of days, worth one breath of its own. Now a small test.

Think back over yesterday's conversations, the kitchen, the office, the group chat. How many were about someone who wasn't there? It's not a trick question, and the answer can be a little uncomfortable.
The handbook's thirty-third section is a long set of small rules for how a person of character talks, laughs and listens. The next few days take it a piece at a time. It starts with the mouth.

teach.h: CHOOSE A CHARACTER, AND KEEP IT.
teach.b: Section thirty-three begins: decide now on a certain character and pattern for yourself, and keep to it, whether you're alone or with other people. Everything after is a sketch of that character.
The first stroke: let silence be the general rule, Epictetus says, or say only what's needed, in few words. That's not a vow of silence. It's a default, like a resting position.

teach.h: SKIP THE GLADIATORS AND HORSE RACES.
teach.b: When you do talk, rarely and when the moment calls for it, skip the ordinary topics: gladiators, horse races, athletes, food and drink. Those were the everyday topics of his world, he implies.
Translate them into today and you'll recognize the list. He isn't banning sports. He's noticing how many hours of a life go into conversation that leaves nobody changed.
Above all, not about people. Don't blame them, don't praise them, don't compare them. That's the one he leans on hardest.
Then a gentler line: if you can, turn your friends' conversation toward something worthwhile, and among strangers, keep quiet. Why would a Stoic care so much?

Talk about absent people is almost always talk about things outside your control: what they did, what they're like, what they deserve. It feeds judgment and envy, and it rarely helps the person being discussed.
Mostly quiet isn't cold. It leaves room for the conversations that matter.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism treat silence as their default in conversation and make a habit of not discussing absent people, especially not blaming, praising or comparing them.

o: silence by default, few words, and not about people
keeping your feelings hidden from everyone
a vow never to speak again, like a hermit's

s: Epictetus asks for a total vow of silence
silence is the general rule; speak when needed, in few words.
he warns against praising absent people, not just blaming them
blaming, praising and comparing are all on his list.

games.q: you're with friends and the talk turns to an absent coworker. what does Epictetus suggest?
o: if you can, turn the talk toward something worthwhile.
games.why: he says to turn friends' conversation toward what's fitting if you can, and among strangers simply to keep quiet.

practice: Let the noise of the day thin out, and picture the moment later when a conversation turns toward someone who isn't there, with its little pull, the thrill of the story.
See yourself letting it pass, saying nothing, or asking the other person how they're doing instead. Then rest in the quiet you're sitting in now.

wordCard.voice: Mostly quiet. Epictetus' first rule for a person of character: silence by default, few words when needed, and not about people. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: silence, which Enchiridion 33 makes the general rule.

carryVoice: Your line: let silence be the rule. Fewer words leave more room to listen. See you tomorrow.
